reasoning: Preserved all three high-priority failure edits, including the operational candidate-slot check and the distinct guidance for visual-identification and flattened-clue prompts. The success edit addresses elliptical fragments without an explicit question, a case not covered by the failure edits, so it is retained as a targeted addition. No edit targets the protected section.

edits.target: For clues linking entities, identify the precise relation and the role of the missing answer before selecting a candidate—for example, a source versus what an instrument measures, or a city represented in an acronym versus the location of a related institution. A candidate's name or topic appearing nearby is not enough: prefer evidence that supports the same relation and the clue's distinguishing details.
edits.content: For visual-identification clues such as “seen here” or “shown here,” do not choose among candidates by generic action-word overlap alone. If several items fit the same action or attribute, compare the full clue against substantive passages and favor evidence that directly identifies the specific item in the described state over an incidental anecdote about a related item.

edits.target: For proper names and titles, use the conventional form that identifies the requested entity. Do not substitute a nickname or later brand name for the historically relevant label, omit words from a work's title when the work is requested, or add optional middle names. Conversely, when the clue requests a generic class, do not embellish it with a narrower associated name.
edits.content:
## Test the Candidate in the Answer Slot
Before finalizing, substitute the candidate into the answer slot implied by the clue. It must match the requested semantic type and granularity—for example, a city rather than a conference held there, an acid rather than an alkaline cleaning agent, or a generic term rather than a named event or source-title phrase. For a term or class, use the answer at that scope; do not promote it to a fuller label unless the clue requests that name. Check that its grammatical form also fits the clue.

edits.target: In noisy or search-style context, a passage may repeat the clue without supplying its answer. Treat that echo as a locator for relevant material, not as evidence for the missing answer; use substantive passages to identify the target and verify distinctive clue details. If the passage explicitly pairs the clue with an answer, it can serve as direct evidence.
edits.content:
## Reconstruct Flattened Clue Prompts
When a question is keyword-like, has lost spaces or punctuation, or comes from a clue archive, do not assume every adjacent word belongs to one phrase. Use the snippet and context to distinguish the clue from category labels, answer-length markers, and neighboring clue text. Identify the requested answer slot and answer that clue, rather than a related entity suggested by surrounding terms.

For an elliptical fragment without an explicit question, reconstruct the omitted relation from substantive context before filling the answer slot—for example, a date-and-place fragment may identify an event or person, while “name before X” asks for an earlier name of X. Resolve references only when the context supports them; do not infer a relation from a bare name or association alone.
